As an Electrical Engineer who actually considered buying a Ford Focus Electric for his daily (and senseless) cross-city commute (to tappity tap commands to servers in a data center that's near his house) the biggest issue is battery technology.

My past cars have lasted me 10 years before repairs and maintenance made them unfavorable compared to an upgrade. With an electric, the battery life is about 5 years - and replacement batteries can cost as much as $10k (or in this case, 1/3 of the new vehicle cost).

I don't know a lot of people stupid enough to buy a car that you need to buy 1/3 of again halfway through it's service life.

I'm hoping that Uber/Apple/Google and the rest of the self-driving car folk get their acts together before I need my next car so I can just summon one of their rides instead of owning a car myself. This will also make it easier to try new fuels since I can just summon a fully charged electric as easily as one powered by gas.

Unfortunately, legislators and the industries that fund them oppose services like Uber - and self-driving cars in general, so mostly political issues stand in their way.

When it happens, we'll need fewer cars, and that will also open up a lot of valuable land currently used for parking for more useful development.

Article is total bullshit, though. Percentages don't tell anything like the whole story.

From the first article, in Europe, "electric vehicle (EV) registrations significantly grew (+53.0%), rising from 18,024 units in Q2 2014 to 27,575 units in Q2 2015." Notice that is per quarter.

Meanwhile, from the second article, "US green-car sales last month fell 17 percent from a year earlier to about 44,569 units. Plug-in vehicle demand did even worse, with sales down 23 percent to about 8,738 units." Notice that is per month.

In other words, more than six times as many of these vehicles are sold in the U.S. than in Europe. Total car sales in Europe and the U.S. are about the same, averaging around 15 million vehicles annually. Which, of course, means that the U.S. has a higher percentage of green vehicles on its roads than Europe does.

Having said all that, the decline in the U.S. is understandable. Fuel prices here are much lower than in Europe, and have been dropping recently, so there is less demand in terms of fuel efficiency. And, Americans typically drive a lot farther than Europeans, and plug-in vehicles don't have the same endurance. So there are lots of reasons Americans aren't all jumping on the bandwagon.
